courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: Tagged pointers: a version counter beside the pointer
md: Tagged pointer = pointer plus a counter compared and swapped as one unit, bumped on every successful CAS. It turns "same value" into "same value and same version".

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Per-query deltas, paired tests and confidence intervals
md: Queries are not the only noise source. If a stage is trained, its score also varies with the random seed. Use the same seeds and checkpoints for every stage you are not ablating, and when the ablated stage itself is retrained, run several seeds and report the spread, or a seed-to-seed swing can masquerade as a component effect.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Sequential vs random ids, and why random ids are not authorization
md: Parler's public posts were meant to be readable one at a time. Sequential ids plus no rate limit turned "anyone can read a post" into "anyone can copy the entire site, with GPS locations". Authorization decides who may read an object; rate limits and unpredictable ids decide how cheaply someone can read all of them. You need both.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: What Active Directory is: one directory for thousands of machines
md: A domain is not a wall. Domains in one forest trust each other automatically, and the Enterprise Admins group of the forest root is an administrator in every domain (next lesson). Plan protection for the whole forest, not one domain at a time.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: AS-REP roasting and password spraying against AD
md: Turning off pre-authentication hands out crackable material to anyone; 4768 with pre-auth type 0 finds it. Spraying hides under per-account lockout; count distinct accounts per source in 4771 and 4776, not failures per account.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Tiered administration, Protected Users and LAPS
md: Tiering fails quietly through agents. A backup, monitoring or patching tool that runs as SYSTEM on DCs, managed from a Tier 1 console, makes that console Tier 0. List everything installed on DCs and everyone who controls it.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: Format string bugs as read and write primitives
md: A format string bug is a primitive factory: the read directives leak, and %n writes. The cure is structural and cheap: constant format strings, enforced by -Werror=format-security and static analysis.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: OPSEC through the defender's eyes: every action leaves a trace
md: Map each emulated step to the log that must record it before the exercise. If the step passes unseen, the gap is in one of three places: the data was never collected, it was collected but no rule looked, or a rule fired and nobody acted. Lesson 12 names these gaps.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: An agent benchmark is a task, an environment and a grader
md: Outcome grading is not the same as correct behavior. A grader only sees what it checks: tests that cover one interpretation, a database diff, an answer string. Anything outside the check (rudeness, a policy step skipped, an unrelated file deleted) can pass silently.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: Keeping the context window under control
md: Compaction is lossy. The Agent SDK docs warn that specific instructions from early in the conversation may not survive a summary. Put durable rules in a file that is re-injected on every request (the SDK uses CLAUDE.md for this), not only in the first user message.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: Evaluating memory and the ways it fails
md: Memory is untrusted input that outlives the session. Record provenance on every write (user said it, a tool returned it, the model inferred it), only promote user-stated facts to instructions-like status, show retrieved memories to the model as quoted data, and give users a way to view and delete what the agent remembers.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: Reward design: hidden tests, partial credit and judges
md: Partial credit is not automatically better. A reward that counts tests which already passed pays the agent for the starting state, so on hard tasks the policy can learn that touching nothing beats trying. Credit only the change you want, and make breaking existing behavior cost something.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: EchoLeak: one email, zero clicks, Copilot leaks
md: Every one of Microsoft's controls existed and every one had a gap. Layered defence only works if each layer is complete on its own: all Markdown syntaxes, all allowlisted domains, all retrieval paths.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Misinformation and unbounded consumption
md: Agents multiply consumption: one user request can trigger many model calls and tool calls in a loop. Cap steps per task and total tokens per task, not only per request, or a confused agent (or an injected one) can run until the budget is gone.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: Generating crystals with diffusion: CDVAE to MatterGen
md: A generator's novelty number is only as good as its reference set and structure matcher. Note that the same disorder issue from the GNoME critique appears here: the synthesized TaCr2O6 was disordered, and MatterGen's ordered-disordered matcher exists so that an ordered variant of a known disordered compound is not counted as new.

courseTitle: Allocation tracing and replay
lessonTitle: What an allocation trace records and why you would replay it
md: Live bytes are not RSS. RSS counts whole pages the process has touched, including allocator metadata, rounding and free holes. The gap between the two is the overhead you are usually hunting.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Local Outlier Factor: density compared with your neighbors
md: scikit-learn's LocalOutlierFactor has two modes. With novelty=False (the default) only fit_predict and negative_outlier_factor_ exist. With novelty=True you get predict, decision_function and score_samples, but the docs warn to call them only on new data: scoring the training points that way gives wrong results, and predict will not match fit_predict.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: API keys, bearer tokens and session cookies
md: An API key in a mobile app or a web page is public. Anyone can unpack the app and read it. Keys that must stay secret belong on servers; a client that runs on the user's device needs a per-user token instead. Defender view: a fixed prefix like `sk_` lets secret scanners find leaked keys in code; log the key id (never the secret) per request and revoke on any leak.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Scopes, consent phishing and refresh token rotation
md: Changing the password does not reliably remove an app's granted consent. RFC 9700 only says servers *may* revoke refresh tokens on a password change, and the consent record itself stays. Response to consent phishing means finding and revoking the app's consent and tokens, not just resetting credentials.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: GraphQL risks: introspection, batching and query depth
md: In GraphQL one request can mean one operation or thousands. Price requests by the work they ask for, check authorization where each field is resolved, and let the server, not the client, decide what is too expensive.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: How static analysis finds bugs: taint from source to sink
md: Source, propagation, sanitiser, sink. A finding is a path from a source to a sink with no sanitiser on it. False positives come from checks the tool cannot understand; false negatives come from sources, sinks or paths it does not model.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Prioritising with CVSS, EPSS and KEV, computed on real CVEs
md: KEV says "exploited now", EPSS says "likely soon", CVSS says "how bad if it happens", and your inventory says "where, how exposed, how important". Rank by evidence of exploitation and exposure first, severity second.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Restart part 1: analysis, then redo that repeats history
md: Redo is decided per page by LSN comparison alone, never by whether the transaction committed. Updates 80 and 100 belong to losers and are redone anyway. After redo the database is exactly as it was at the crash, and only then does undo begin.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Testing input types on your own data
md: Never assume the input type is right because results look plausible. Measure the grid of query and document settings on your own labeled queries, and keep tests that fail loudly when a call site or the index metadata drifts.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Inside Tokio's scheduler: local queues, stealing, LIFO slot
md: Tokio guarantees fairness only in a weak sense: if the number of tasks is bounded and no task blocks, every woken task is eventually scheduled. It does **not** promise round-robin order. Two ready tasks A and B may see A scheduled five times before B, even if A calls `yield_now`, a future that returns `Pending` once after arranging its own wakeup, so the scheduler may run something else first.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: From a waveform to 0.96 s log-mel patches
md: Clip length does not map to patches by simple division. YAMNet needs at least 0.975 s of audio (0.96 s plus the rest of the last 25 ms STFT window), pads anything shorter with silence, and rounds longer audio up to a whole hop. Our script gets 1 patch for 0.5 s, **2 patches for 1.0 s**, 10 for 5 s and 20 for 10 s.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Storing passwords wrong: plaintext, encryption, fast hashes
md: Hashing is not encryption. If a company can email you your old password, it is stored in plaintext or reversibly encrypted. A hash with no salt is only slightly better than plaintext against an attacker with a list of common passwords.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Kinds of MFA, and the maths inside a TOTP code
md: A TOTP code proves you hold the shared secret right now. It does not prove which website you are typing it into: anyone who sees the code within its 30-second window can use it once. Lesson 12 exploits exactly that gap.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Tracking sources and checking every citation
md: A citation that exists is not a citation that supports. Checking that every URL resolves catches invented sources but misses the more common failure: a real page cited for a claim it does not make.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: Below the API: Inferentia, Trainium, Neuron and SageMaker AI
md: Moving work onto Inferentia or Trainium is a **compiler** project as much as a hardware choice: your model must compile with Neuron, and custom ops may need NKI kernels. Budget engineering time for that, not just instance price.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Why a pipelined CPU has to guess at every branch
md: Speculation is not a correctness risk for your program: wrong-path results never reach registers or memory. It is only a time cost. (It can leak information through caches, which is the Spectre family of attacks; lesson 5 touches on that.)

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: The LSM write path: memtable, flush and immutable SSTables
md: Misconception: "a delete in an LSM-tree frees space immediately." It adds data: a tombstone. Space comes back only when compaction merges the tombstone with every older version of that key and can finally drop both.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: Sequential flooding: how one scan wipes out the hot set
md: Recency alone cannot tell a hot page from a page that was just read once. Every scan-resistant policy adds some second signal: a count, a second reference, or knowledge of which query read the page.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Availability engineering: nines, redundancy and failure domains
md: Nines from a vendor apply to the vendor's component, under its definition of "available". Your service's availability is lower: it multiplies every hard dependency, and redundancy only helps for failures that do not hit all copies at once.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Backups attackers cannot reach: immutability and isolated recovery
md: Immutable storage is not an immutable backup *system*. If the same admin can change retention for future backups, delete the encryption key, disable the backup jobs or lock everyone out of the console, the attacker wins slowly instead of quickly. Protect the policies, keys and access paths as carefully as the bytes.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Exercising the plan: tabletops, functional tests, failovers and chaos
md: Climb from training to tabletop, functional exercise, full switchover test and continuous chaos experiments. Each needs objectives, success criteria and measured results; the output is a list of gaps with owners, and the measured RTO replaces the guessed one in the plan.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Generating with patches: the BLT decoding loop and its real cost
md: The BLT paper is explicit: its FLOP matching is theoretical, and its implementation may not yet match tokenizer-based models in wall-clock time. Equal FLOPs per byte is a claim about arithmetic, not about latency at batch size 1.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Data races: pthreads in C versus Send and Sync in Rust
md: Implementing Send or Sync by hand is `unsafe impl Send for MyType {}`, one of the five powers in lesson 4. The compiler cannot check it, and the Rustonomicon warns that an incorrect implementation can cause undefined behavior: you are promising that every way to reach the type from two threads is synchronized.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Why one load can cost 3 cycles or 240
md: You never call the cache. The only levers you have are **which addresses you touch and in what order**: data layout and access pattern. That is what the rest of this course makes precise.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Why tracing circuits needs a replacement model
md: Attribution graphs trade the real model for an interpretable stand-in whose direct interactions are linear on one prompt. Every claim read off the graph is a hypothesis about the real model until an intervention confirms it.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Inverse propensity scoring turns clicks into unbiased labels
md: Only clicked documents need propensities, and the estimate is unbiased only if the propensities are correct and every relevant document has a nonzero chance of being observed. Joachims et al. also require that propensities depend only on logged information (unconfoundedness).

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Framework auto-escaping and its escape hatches
md: "It comes from our own API" is not the same as "trusted". The value was typed by some user before your API stored it. React's own Markdown example is safe only because the rendered HTML is shown back to the same user who wrote it, and because the team trusts the Markdown parser to have no bugs.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: Temperature: why CLIP multiplies cosines by up to 100
md: The temperature turns a ranking of small cosine gaps into a confident probability. Its value decides how sharply the loss concentrates on hard negatives, which is why CLIP learns it and caps the logit scale at 100 for stability.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Your own rules: key abuse, persistence and log tampering
md: Misconception: "ATT&CK IDs are permanent". MITRE reorganises the matrix: Disable or Modify Cloud Log moved from T1562.008 to T1685.002, and tactics have been renamed. Map rules to IDs, but review the mapping when a new ATT&CK version ships.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Code Spaces 2014: why one account is one blast radius
md: Design as if any one credential will be stolen tomorrow. The test of an architecture is not "can an attacker get in?" but "what can one stolen login destroy or read?" Keep the data and its last good copy behind different identities, in different accounts.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Azure in depth: role assignments, Run Command and PIM
md: In Azure, the keys to escalation are writing role assignments and running code where a privileged identity lives. Make powerful roles eligible through PIM, delegate assignments with conditions instead of Owner, and treat Virtual Machine Contributor on a VM as equal to that VM's managed identity.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Long-lived keys vs temporary credentials: STS and Uber 2016
md: Prefer roles and temporary credentials everywhere. AWS's own best practices say to require human users to use federation with temporary credentials and to require workloads to use IAM roles. Long-term access keys are for the few cases nothing else supports, and they need rotation, monitoring and the narrowest possible permissions.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: What k-means actually optimises
md: Scaling is a modelling choice, not a cleanup step. Standardising says "one standard deviation of every feature counts the same", which silently gives a noisy, unimportant feature as much say as a crucial one. Decide how much each feature should weigh, then scale to match. k-means, DBSCAN's eps and every method in this course measure distance, and none of them is scale free.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Evaluating a clustering with and without labels
md: Look at the first two bars. The k = 2 clustering with the *better* inertia, 28.8333, scores ARI 0.4109, while the local optimum with the worse inertia, 30.4167, scores 0.7734. Optimising the objective harder moved the answer away from the truth. Inertia is a proxy, and this is what it means for a proxy to be imperfect: never argue from inertia to correctness.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: SIMD, compiled queries and where columnar engines hit limits
md: Columnar storage cuts bytes moved; vectorized execution cuts instructions per byte. SIMD multiplies the second only when data is dense and in cache.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Why code breaks at -O2: undefined behavior as an optimization license
md: The optimizer assumes the program has no UB: signed overflow never happens, differently typed pointers never alias, dereferenced pointers are not null. Code that breaks those rules can change behavior at -O2. Find it with sanitizers and the -fwrapv, -fno-strict-aliasing and -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks switches, then fix the code.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: The observe-act loop: screenshots in, mouse and keyboard out
md: A computer-use agent is an ordinary agent loop where the tool is "the computer" and the observation is a screenshot. The model proposes actions in screenshot pixel coordinates; the harness executes them, and is the only place you can enforce scaling, safety and verification.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: How loom takes over the scheduler and walks every schedule
md: loom only sees what goes through loom types. A `std::sync::Mutex` or a third-party lock inside your code still runs, but loom cannot schedule around it, so executions that are possible in reality are silently not modeled. Libraries you depend on need loom support too for full coverage.

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: iCT, sCM, LCM and the other few-step distillers
md: Consistency models learn the end of the ODE trajectory, not its slope. The boundary condition anchors the chain at the data; adjacent-time agreement (from a teacher's ODE step or from the data itself) propagates it to high noise; extra steps re-noise and jump again to trade compute for quality.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: The hash ring: each key goes to the next node clockwise
md: Consistent hashing minimises *movement*. It does not by itself give *balance*. With one random token per node, arcs vary wildly in size, as the toy ring shows. The next lesson fixes that.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Why scheduling explodes, and what a constraint model is
md: A constraint solver separates **what** a solution is (the model) from **how** to find it (the search). You declare variables, domains and constraints; the solver chooses the order of guesses and the deductions. Adding a rule means adding one constraint, not rewriting a search loop.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: One kernel, many tenants: the container threat model
md: A container is a fenced process on a shared kernel. Threat-model it as "attacker has a shell in this process" and ask which credentials, network paths and kernel interfaces that shell can touch.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: The API server is the front door: authn, authz, admission
md: Every request passes authentication (401 if unknown), authorization (403 if not allowed), then admission (mutate, then validate) before etcd. Reads skip admission, so RBAC alone protects them. Turn on audit logging, because it is off unless you configure it.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Network policies: from default allow to default deny
md: Pods are non-isolated until a policy selects them. Start each namespace with default deny for both directions, add DNS, then add one allow per intended connection, on both sides.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a hardening map and where to practise
md: No single control holds. Minimal signed images, Restricted pods, least-privilege RBAC, default-deny networks, encrypted and narrowly readable Secrets, authenticated node APIs, patched runtimes, and two kinds of detection: each covers what the others miss.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Resolving the second one and those against what was shown
md: Do not ask the LLM to copy job ids out of text. Give it the shown list with positions and attributes and let it output a position or an attribute match; code does the lookup. A model that types ids can produce a well-formed id that was never shown.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Do reasoning models admit the hints they use?
md: When the model can act on information without reasoning about it, its CoT usually stays silent about it, even with no pressure to hide. CoT monitoring then helps you notice frequent behaviors, but it cannot certify that a behavior is absent.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Why a reranker reads the query and the document together
md: A cross-encoder is not a better embedding model. It has no vector output you could store in a vector database. If someone asks you to index a corpus with a reranker, the answer is that you cannot: the score exists only for a specific query.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: What cryptography promises, and to whom
md: Ask of every design: which of confidentiality, integrity and authenticity do I need, against whom, and where does the key live? A primitive that gives one goal never silently gives the others.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Randomness: where keys come from, and the Debian disaster
md: A random-looking output says nothing about its entropy. Debian's weak keys passed every visual check; their weakness was only visible by counting how many could exist.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: From MMA atoms to TiledMMA and TiledCopy
md: Atoms are hardware facts, TiledMMA and TiledCopy are spatial arrangements of atoms, and partition_A/B/C or partition_S/D (source and destination) turn a tile into per-thread fragments. Swapping the atom (FMA, mma.sync, wgmma) changes the instruction without rewriting the loops.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Worked example: what a CXL access costs
md: Do not assume every CXL device behaves like Pond's model. Sun et al. measured three real devices: one had load latency only 35% longer than a remote-socket DDR5 node, while the other two were about 2x and 3x longer. Their bandwidth efficiency also differed widely by controller. Emulating CXL with a remote NUMA socket, as early research did, can mislead in both directions.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Van Buren (2021): gates up or down, not good or bad motives
md: Van Buren is not a licence. Misusing data you may open can still be fraud, a privacy violation, a breach of contract, a firing offence or a state crime (lesson 4). And it says nothing about getting past a gate that is down: guessing a password or exploiting a bug to reach an area is still the off-limits kind.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Writing and selling tools: Marcus Hutchins and dual-use code
md: Writing security tools is legal almost everywhere. Laws target tools designed primarily for crime and people who supply them intending, or believing likely, criminal use. Context is evidence: who you sell to, how you advertise, what the features are for.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Evidence in court: authenticity, hearsay and chain of custody
md: Courts ask: is it what you say it is (authenticity), was it made routinely at the time (business records), and who could have changed it (chain of custody)? Automatic logs, hashes at collection and a tamper-evident custody record answer all three.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: The 3-step pipeline and what it did to The Pile
md: Using 280M-proxy weights for an 8B model is an empirical bet that good weights transfer across a 30x jump in scale. It paid off here, but the paper lists why weights transfer, and how far, as open questions, and its 1B proxy produced a worse 8B model than the 280M one (lesson 6). Weights also assume a token budget: lesson 5 shows what happens when you reuse them for a longer run.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Cleaning the crawl: heuristic rules, perplexity filters, exact dedup
md: Clean before you mix. Cheap rules remove describable junk, a perplexity filter keeps text resembling a reference (with its biases), and exact plus near deduplication removes copies. Each step shrinks domains, so redo the epoch math of lesson 5 and rerun the mixing step on the cleaned data.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Choosing a layout: hot/cold splits, ECS chunks and columnar data
md: List the hot loops, write down which fields each one touches and whether it streams or jumps, then pick the layout that packs those bytes together. Re-measure when the access pattern changes.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Tokens and masks: taking real values out of systems
md: Dynamic masking changes what is displayed, not what can be queried. Against anyone who can write their own WHERE clauses it is not a security boundary; use column permissions (lesson 8), tokens or encryption there.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a data security programme, and practice
md: Data security is a loop: find, label, keep less, protect, watch, destroy, with each finding feeding back into the inventory. Measure each stage, and judge controls by who can still cause the data to be read.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Replaying failures, the limits of DST, and who uses it
md: DST turns rare, timing-dependent bugs into seeds. The engineering cost is up front (every source of nondeterminism behind an interface, plus good oracles), and the return is that every bug found is a bug you can replay and fix.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a secure pipeline, a response plan, practice
md: The question to ask of every part of a pipeline: who can change what this runs, and what can it reach when it does? If the answer to the first is "anyone who can open a PR" and to the second is "production", there is a gap, however many scanners run.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Why prefill stalls decode on a shared GPU
md: Prefill is compute-bound and sets TTFT; decode is memory-bound and sets TPOT. Putting both in one batch makes each phase pay for the other.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: From sectors to partitions to image files
md: Do not stop at the partitions. NIST SP 800-86 counts *free space* (areas not allocated to any partition, including whole deleted volumes) as a place where data may remain. Our lab disk already has 2,047 sectors before the first partition that no file system owns.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Anti-forensics from the defender's side: what each trick leaves
md: The cleanup is evidence too. A 1102 event, a reset journal or deleted shadow copies at 14:35 tell you someone with administrator rights was covering tracks then, which often dates the intrusion better than anything they deleted.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Why DPO skips the reward model and the RL loop
md: DPO is not "RLHF without a reward". It fits the same Bradley-Terry reward model, just parameterized through the policy. It also inherits the KL objective's $\beta$. What it removes is the separate reward network and on-policy sampling during training.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Why a live data migration needs four careful phases
md: Turning on dual writes does not make the stores identical. It only covers objects written *after* the switch. Objects that are never updated again stay only in the old store until the backfill copies them.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Why run your tracing logic inside the kernel
md: eBPF lets you run your own logic at the moment an event happens, inside the kernel, with a load-time proof that it cannot crash or hang the machine. bpftrace makes that a one-liner: probe, optional filter, action, and maps that summarize in the kernel.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Fewer operations and fewer weights, then shipping it
md: Pruning does not automatically make a model smaller or faster. The LiteRT docs state that pruned models are the same size on disk and have the same latency; they only compress better. You get size savings from a sparse format or compression, and speed only from kernels or hardware that skip zeros. With 8-bit values plus 8-bit gaps, sparse storage only wins once more than half the weights are zero.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: PAN-OS GlobalProtect, 2024: a cookie that became a command
md: Early interim guidance can be wrong. The first CVE-2024-3400 advisory tied exposure to telemetry; that was later corrected. Use a vendor workaround to buy hours, then install the fix and verify, rather than treating the workaround as the answer.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Measuring wasted tokens and training them away
md: Plain SFT on short samples barely helped here (a 2.0% cut on MATH500). Imitating short traces is weaker than contrasting short against long, because the model never sees what it should move away from.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Where a sensor sits: kernel callbacks, minifilters and network filters
md: Misconception: "kernel mode makes a sensor untouchable." A kernel sensor can see everything, but so can any other code that reaches the kernel. An attacker who loads their own driver, or abuses a vulnerable signed one, is on equal footing with the sensor. That is exactly what the EDR-killer lesson covers.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Credential hardening: LAPS, LSA protection and Credential Guard
md: These controls each close one path: LAPS stops one local password from opening every machine; LSA protection stops ordinary processes reading LSASS; Credential Guard keeps the most reusable secrets out of LSASS's reach entirely; the ASR LSASS rule covers machines that can run neither. Check they are actually running, not just configured.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Scoring a disaggregation: MAE, NEP, NDE and F1
md: Metric details change numbers silently. The on/off threshold (10 W in NILMTK) sets F1; whether a paper reports NEP, NDE or energy accuracy changes which appliances look good; and per-appliance averages weight a lamp and a kettle equally while energy accuracy is dominated by the kettle. Always state the metric definition alongside a number.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: From pairwise links to entities: clustering
md: Blocking decides which pairs are compared, scoring decides which pairs are linked, and clustering decides which records share an ID. Tune the threshold on labeled data, because it trades false merges against missed merges.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Delegated vs application permissions, and who may consent
md: Misconception: an attacker needs an admin to consent before an app can steal mail. Delegated mail and file permissions are user-consentable by default, and the user's own mailbox is often the prize. Admin consent is needed for the tenant-wide versions, which is why attackers who compromise an admin go straight for application permissions.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Devices and the Primary Refresh Token: SSO bound to hardware
md: Misconception: a device-based Conditional Access rule means only company laptops get in. It means the token request came with a valid device identity. A device an attacker registers is a real device object, which is why device registration and join rights should be restricted and new registrations reviewed.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Taking over admins: help desks, MFA resets and rogue federation
md: Misconception: after a help-desk takeover, resetting the victim's password and MFA again evicts the attacker. If the attacker federated a domain or added an app credential, they can mint access without that account. Check federation settings, app credentials, role assignments and registered devices before calling it contained.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Level-triggered versus edge-triggered, and reading until EAGAIN
md: Closing a descriptor removes it from the interest list only when **every** descriptor referring to the same open file is closed. If a `dup` or a `fork` left another copy open, events can keep arriving for a number you already closed. Call `EPOLL_CTL_DEL` before closing when duplicates may exist.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Confidence intervals by bootstrapping over queries
md: Resample queries, keep each query's pair of scores together, and report the interval along with the mean. A CI that crosses zero means your query set cannot tell the systems apart, whatever the point estimate says.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Why one leaked pointer defeats ASLR, and guessing at scale
md: ASLR is a secret, and like any secret it fails when leaked or when there are too few bits to stop guessing. Count the bits, avoid restart patterns that keep the secret constant, and treat information leaks as the first half of an exploit.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Fixing it: pad, align, or stop sharing writes
md: A fix needs both size and alignment: each hot item must start on a line boundary and be at least a line long. And pad only data that different threads write often; group everything else tightly.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: What the server sees: secure aggregation, DP, and Flower
md: The one thing to remember: federated learning is an optimization algorithm shaped by a systems constraint. Every piece (averaging instead of gradient sharing, a quorum instead of a barrier, masks instead of raw updates, noise instead of trust) exists because rounds are expensive, clients are unreliable, and the server is not allowed to look.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Aux-loss-free balancing: steer the router with a bias
md: The bias changes **which** experts a token uses, never **how much** a chosen expert contributes, and it receives no gradient. That is how Loss-Free Balancing controls load without fighting the language-modeling objective.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Tile sizes, GQA head fusion and JIT attention variants
md: FlashInfer = one block-sparse view of every KV layout, attention states merged exactly so work can be split and composed freely, a per-step plan that balances skewed lengths while staying CUDA-graph friendly, and a JIT template so new variants get fused kernels instead of new libraries.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Inductive invariants: from bounded checks to every N
md: An invariant is true in reachable states; an inductive invariant is preserved from *any* state that satisfies it. Model checking finds the first; proofs need the second. Use TLC or Apalache to debug a candidate before you try to prove it. Verus loop invariants, later in the course, carry the same three obligations.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Connecting specs to running code, and the wider tool map
md: Trace validation is testing, not proof: it checks only the runs you logged, and its verdict depends on choosing the right points in the code to log each atomic step. The paper says plainly that it does not provide formal correctness guarantees. Its strength is that it keeps a spec honest at the cost of logging.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Microscaling: one power-of-two scale per 32 values
md: MX formats move fine-grained scaling into hardware: 32 elements share one power-of-two E8M0 scale, applied by the tensor core during the dot product. For 8-bit elements that works well. For 4-bit elements the power-of-two restriction can waste up to a whole binade of FP4's tiny 3.58-binade range.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Trading latency for throughput: commit_delay and async commit
md: `synchronous_commit = off` and `fsync = off` sound similar but are not. The first may lose the last ~600 ms (by default) of acknowledged commits and stays consistent. The second can corrupt the whole cluster (PostgreSQL's word for all the databases one server manages) and is only for data you can recreate, such as an initial bulk load.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Measuring fuzzers honestly: coverage, crashes and statistics
md: "Unique crashes" is not a bug count. When a tool, a vendor pitch or your own dashboard reports it, ask how deduplication was done and how many distinct fixes the crashes needed.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: AI-assisted vulnerability discovery: what is verified so far
md: Verified so far: AI agents can find real bugs by variant analysis (Big Sleep, SQLite), AI-written harnesses extend fuzzing coverage and find real CVEs (OSS-Fuzz, OpenSSL), and attackers use AI to find logic flaws (GTIG 2026). In every defensive case, a concrete reproducer and a sanitizer or test confirmed the bug.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Levenshtein automata, SymSpell and fuzzy queries in production
md: Lucene's javadoc documents a surprise: `FuzzyQuery` on `abcd` with `maxEdits=2` does not match the indexed term `ab`, even though the Levenshtein distance is 2. Engines add rules of their own on top of the textbook distance, so test short terms and other edge cases directly.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: From an accepted match to a WCS header, and the triangle alternative
md: A match is not the end product. The solver turns matched star pairs into CRPIX, CRVAL and a CD matrix under a TAN projection, which any FITS tool can then use to label every pixel with RA and Dec.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Resize: the half-pixel center, worked on a four-pixel row
md: A common misconception is that interpolation conventions only matter for image quality. They also move geometry. If training resized with half-pixel centers and inference resizes without them, every pixel coordinate the model predicts is offset by $(s-1)/2$ source pixels, and no amount of retraining the head (the final prediction layers) fixes a preprocessing mismatch.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Streams: when a freed block is safe to reuse
md: Forgetting record_stream (or calling s0.wait_stream(s1) before the free, which makes all later work on s0 wait for the work already queued on s1) is a silent data race, not a crash: the new tensor's kernel on s0 may overwrite memory that s1 is still reading. The PyTorch docs note the synchronization is needed even when the side stream only writes.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Misalignment, strides and effective bandwidth
md: **Misconception:** the L1 cache makes access patterns irrelevant. Caches help when nearby warps reuse what was over-fetched, as with small misalignments. A large stride over data read once gets no reuse, and every unused byte still crosses the DRAM interface.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Occupancy: what it buys and what caps it
md: Occupancy is a capability, not an achievement. 100 percent occupancy with 5 percent of peak throughput is a latency-bound kernel with plenty of warps and nothing for them to do, and the fix has nothing to do with occupancy.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: Occupancy: how many warps fit on an SM at once
md: Higher occupancy is not automatically faster. Low occupancy hurts latency hiding, but past some point extra warps add nothing, and a lower-occupancy kernel can keep more data in registers and avoid spilling (storing values that do not fit in registers out in slower memory). Measure.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: What GraphRAG costs and how its gains were measured
md: Do not estimate GraphRAG cost from the number of documents alone. Cost scales with total tokens, chunk size, gleaning rounds, the number of entities and relationships that need summaries, and the number of communities. The official docs open with a warning that GraphRAG can consume a lot of LLM resources and suggest starting small.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: DeepSeek-R1-Zero and R1: RLVR with GRPO at scale
md: The split in R1 is telling: verifiable rewards where answers can be checked (math, code, logic), learned reward models only where they cannot, and those kept short because they get hacked.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: Why a flame graph shows where time goes but not why
md: A higher IPC is not automatically better. A thread spinning on a lock retires instructions quickly, so it shows high IPC while making no logical progress. Judge IPC together with the instruction count and the run time.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Mitigations, their costs, and checking a real machine
md: `mitigations=off` is sometimes recommended in benchmark blogs. On any machine that runs code you do not fully trust (a browser, CI jobs, containers from others, VMs of other tenants), that trades a few percent of speed for letting that code read memory it should not. Measure your workload first; most of the cost is concentrated in system-call-heavy paths.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Transparent Huge Pages: faults, khugepaged and memory bloat
md: The synchronous stall is the classic THP latency spike. `/proc/vmstat` counts it: `compact_stall` increments every time a process stalls to run compaction, with `compact_success` and `compact_fail` alongside. A rising `compact_stall` next to tail-latency spikes is a strong hint. Tail latency is the time of the slowest requests, such as the 99th percentile, called p99.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Serving a hybrid: prefix caching, rollback and chunked prefill
md: A recurrent state is compact but not divisible. Every serving feature that cuts a cache at an arbitrary token (sharing a prefix, rejecting speculative tokens, pausing a prefill) needs a saved state at that exact position or a recomputation from an earlier one. Plan where states are checkpointed the way you plan KV memory.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: The HyDE pipeline: generate, encode, average, search
md: Common misconception: HyDE shows the user the generated passage. It does not. The hypothetical document only becomes a vector; everything returned is a real document from the corpus. Hallucinations (fluent but false details) can still hurt, but by moving the vector, not by being displayed.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Modbus/TCP byte by byte, and why it trusts everyone
md: Encryption alone would not fix this. If any host can still connect and is trusted once connected, encrypting the write just hides the attack from your monitor. What is missing is authentication and authorisation of the sender, which Modbus/TCP Security adds (lesson 7).

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Segmentation, DMZs, one-way gateways and allowlisting
md: Segment so that the office cannot reach the controllers, pass data out through a DMZ (one way where possible), let in remote support only through an approved, timed, MFA-protected door, and keep the safety system off every routed path.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Validating a SAML response: every check, and the replay cache
md: Do not write this yourself for production. Use a maintained SAML library, configure it strictly (signed assertions required, exact Audience and ACS URL, no IdP-initiated login unless needed) and patch it quickly: lesson 7 is about a widely used library that had a critical flaw in step 5. The toy here exists to make each check visible.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: IdP compromise and Golden SAML: forging the whole federation
md: A valid signature proves possession of a key, not that the IdP made a decision. Once the key or the trust list is in an attacker's hands, every SP check passes, so defence moves to protecting the IdP like a domain controller and to correlating SP logins with IdP issuance.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Access reviews and certification: asking again, and meaning it
md: A completed review is not the same as a working control. 100% approved in two seconds per item is evidence that a form was filled in.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Why change detection must align images first
md: Alignment comes before differencing, always. Without it, the change mask mostly measures camera motion, concentrated on every edge in the image.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Events, alerts and incidents: when does it become an incident?
md: Declaring is a decision with consequences: it starts the plan, assigns an incident commander and may start legal clocks. Write the criteria down beforehand so that nobody has to be brave at 2 a.m.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Windows artefacts: event logs, Prefetch, Amcache, Shimcache, MFT
md: A Shimcache or Amcache entry alone does not prove the program ran. Mandiant showed Shimcache entries created just by browsing a folder on some Windows versions. Look for corroboration: Prefetch, 4688, Sysmon, EDR telemetry.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: When data becomes code: the one idea behind every injection
md: The fix for every injection is the same idea: keep code and data in **separate channels**, so the interpreter never has to guess which is which. For SQL that is a parameterised query, for the shell an argument list, for templates a template variable. Escaping and filtering are fallbacks for when no separate channel exists.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Two shared rings: SQEs, CQEs, head and tail
md: If the tail update becomes visible before the SQE fields, the kernel can read a half-written request (say, the right opcode with a stale fd). This is a real bug class in hand-rolled ring code. liburing (Axboe's helper library, lesson 3) does the barriers for you, which is the main reason to use it even if you want raw control elsewhere.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Prototypes: where a missing property comes from
md: Reading a missing property silently falls through to the prototype chain, ending at Object.prototype, which nearly every object shares. The keys `__proto__` and `constructor` (then `prototype`) lead from an ordinary object to that shared object. `Object.create(null)` objects have no chain to follow.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Middleware and internal headers: the Next.js bypass
md: Headers that mean something internally (recursion markers, "already authenticated", forwarded client IPs) must either be stripped at the edge or carry proof that only your own infrastructure can produce. And never let one layer be the only authorisation check: Vercel's own advice is not to use middleware as "the sole method of protecting routes".

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: Cross-thread frees, idle caches and returning memory
md: Published benchmarks (including those in mimalloc's README and report) measure specific workloads. Allocator rankings change with object sizes, thread counts and cross-thread patterns. Measure throughput, p99 latency (the 99th percentile: the time that 99 percent of requests beat) and RSS (resident set size, the memory actually held in RAM) on your own service, with production-like load, before and after switching.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Why the winner changes when the shape changes
md: A common bug is a tuning cache keyed on the kernel name alone, or on batch size only. It never misses, so it never re-tunes, and it silently serves a configuration chosen for a different shape. The symptom is a kernel that is fast in the benchmark that tuned it and mediocre everywhere else.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: Worked example: how SPDK reaches 10 million IOPS on one thread
md: Measure with the right tool. SPDK reports up to 2.6 times more IOPS per core using its own `perf` example tool than using fio (the Flexible I/O Tester, the standard Linux storage benchmark) with the SPDK plugin for 4 KiB random reads, because fio's flexibility costs cycles. A slow benchmark harness can hide a fast driver.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Why a teacher's soft targets beat one-hot labels
md: The teacher's knowledge is its input-to-output mapping, including how much probability it gives to each wrong answer. Distillation transfers that mapping by using the teacher's full output distribution as the training target.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Distilling language models: word-level and sequence-level
md: Word-level KD matches the teacher's full next-token distribution at every position of a fixed sequence and needs its probabilities. Seq-KD trains on the teacher's own output text with plain cross-entropy and needs only text. Both train on prefixes the student did not write.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Sharing keys and values across heads: MQA and GQA
md: GQA does not reduce attention FLOPs per query head: each query head still scores every cached token. It reduces the bytes stored and read, which is what decode is bound by.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Compressing long prompts (SnapKV, PyramidKV) and choosing a recipe
md: Smaller caches only become speed if the attention kernel reads the compressed form directly. Dequantizing to BF16 in a separate pass gives back most of the memory traffic saved.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Eviction and placement: what stays, what sinks, what is dropped
md: Choose eviction by reuse pattern, not habit. LRU is a fine default; workloads with known future reuse (queued multi-turn sessions, scheduled agent steps) do much better with placement driven by the scheduler.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Why one vector per document leaves accuracy behind
md: Late interaction = independent encoding (so documents are precomputed) + token-level matching at query time (so fine-grained evidence is not averaged away into one vector).

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: The continuous thought: hidden state in, hidden state out
md: Misconception: a continuous thought is not the embedding of the most likely next word. It is never rounded to any vocabulary entry. Decoding it with the LM head is a diagnostic only.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: An index is a model: predicting where a key sits
md: A learned index does not return approximate answers. It finds exactly the same record a B-tree would. Only the *path* to the record is approximate; the final local search makes the answer exact.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: From MLM logits to one weight per vocabulary term
md: Misconception: the expansion terms are synonyms. They are whatever the MLM head plus ranking training found useful. The paper's own example document about bow legs gains *leg* and *treatment*, but also *arrow* (bow and arrow) and *teeth*, with small weights.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: LambdaMART in practice: libraries, truncation and click bias
md: In production, LambdaMART is the training objective of a tree ensemble that rescores the top candidates of a first-stage retriever. Its quality depends on labels (judgments or debiased clicks), query-grouped data, and a truncation level that matches the positions users see.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: One family, many transitions: RetNet to GLA, Mamba2, RWKV-7, KDA
md: To place a new linear-attention layer, ask two questions. What is $A_t$: identity, scalar, diagonal, identity minus rank 1, or diagonal plus low rank? And what does the write minimize: a dot-product reward (additive) or a regression error (delta)? Richer $A_t$ means finer forgetting and a costlier kernel.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Processes, PIDs, process trees and signals
md: Read processes as a tree. Who started a process (its parent, its user, its command line in `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`) usually tells you more than its name, because names are trivial to fake.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: What an intruder touches: persistence and where defenders look
md: Do not investigate a live compromise only with the compromised system's own tools if you can avoid it: an intruder with root can alter `ps`, `ls` or the logs. Cross-check with package verification, a trusted copy of the tools, or off-host data.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Measuring a service sandbox with systemd-analyze security
md: `systemd-analyze security` turns sandboxing into a number you can track per unit and gate in CI with `--offline=yes --threshold=`. Lower is better, but the score covers only systemd's own settings and cannot tell you what the service legitimately needs.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Falco: turning the system call stream into alerts
md: Falco = driver (modern eBPF by default) + state + YAML rules (condition, output, priority, macros, lists). It detects, it does not block. Every exclusion you add is a deliberate blind spot; write it down.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Patching a fleet: automatic updates, restarts, reboots and rings
md: Automate installation (unattended-upgrades, dnf-automatic), automate restarts (needrestart), schedule reboots or livepatch urgent kernel fixes, roll out in rings with canaries, and verify the running version, not the package database.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Judge biases: position, verbosity and self-preference
md: For pointwise relevance grades the order bias has an analogue: grading many passages in one prompt lets earlier passages anchor later ones. Grade one passage per call, as the Bing and UMBRELA prompts do, or randomise and repeat if you batch.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Threat model: how an LLM app gets attacked or goes wrong
md: OWASP's top LLM risk guidance says it is unclear whether fool-proof prevention of prompt injection exists, and recommends treating the model as an untrusted user. Design so that a fully hijacked model still cannot do much damage: least-privilege tools (each tool gets only the permissions its job needs), human approval for high-risk actions, and checks outside the model.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Fragmentation, and block tables as page tables
md: Paging does not shrink the KV cache. A 1,500-token sequence still needs 1,500 tokens of K and V. Paging removes the memory that held *nothing*, which is why the gain is largest when requests are short relative to their maximum length.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Constrained decoding: masking logits with a state machine
md: Constrained decoding does not make the model understand the format. It removes the illegal choices at each step and lets the model choose among what is left. An FSM state tells you which tokens are legal; a precomputed index makes that lookup cheap.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Evaluating the parser with exact match per field
md: Errors are not equal. A **spurious** filter (q6's remote_ok, q7's required javascript) removes good results and the user never sees them. A **missing** filter only returns extra results the user can see and skip. Track precision and recall of slots separately and weight spurious filters as the worse error.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Distilled 7B rerankers versus a cross-encoder: choosing a design
md: Write the cost model before choosing the method: calls on the critical path, input tokens, output tokens, and model size. Then check quality on your own queries: the cheapest design that holds your NDCG@10 wins.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Managed routing in Amazon Bedrock, and how routers fail
md: Routing failures are silent. A wrong answer from the weak model looks like any other answer, and the dashboard shows only that costs went down. Log the routed model with every response (Bedrock returns it), and compare quality by route, not just overall.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: RANSAC: keeping only matches that agree on one homography
md: A homography is only correct for planar scenes or pure camera rotation. For a general 3D scene seen from two positions, matches satisfy a fundamental or essential matrix instead, and forcing a homography will reject many correct matches.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Freeing nodes safely: hazard pointers and epochs
md: EBR is fast because readers only write their own epoch when they pin, but it is not strictly lock-free for memory: Fraser notes that a process that stalls inside a critical region stops the limbo lists (Fraser's name for the per-epoch garbage bags) from ever being reclaimed. Hazard pointers bound the unreclaimed memory (at most NR nodes) at the cost of publishing and re-validating every pointer before use.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Drift when a release changes the format, and a pipeline that holds
md: The whole course in one line: a log template is the cheapest useful abstraction over log text, and the only one that turns an unbounded stream of unique strings into a small set of countable events. Everything after it, counting, baselining, sequence models, dashboards, inherits both its power and its errors.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Sigma: one rule format, many SIEMs
md: A converted query is only as right as its pipeline's field mapping. If your SIEM stores Sysmon in a different source, or the 4688 field is NewProcessName rather than Image, the query is valid, runs, and silently matches nothing. Always test converted rules against real events from your own environment.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Position Interpolation and NTK-aware scaling
md: Uniform interpolation protects the slow pairs but blurs the fast ones. Every better method since PI is about treating pairs differently according to their wavelength.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Depth without parameters: what looping a block buys
md: Looping saves **parameters** (memory, communication), not **compute**. Every loop is another full pass through the block, and the passes are sequential, so a $(1 \otimes 12)$ model is about as slow per token as a 12-layer model. Looped models trade memory for depth, they do not make inference free.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Build it: loop your GPT with input injection and random depth
md: Turning a GPT into a recurrent-depth model takes a split into prelude, core and coda, a concat adapter, a noise start and a random-depth training loop. The monitor that matters is the gap between low-r and high-r validation loss.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: Counting parameters, choosing targets, merging for free inference
md: Merging has a price: a merged model serves one adapter. Hu et al. note it is not straightforward to batch requests for *different* adapters in one forward pass once A and B are folded into W. Serving many adapters at once needs the unmerged form, which is the subject of the multi-LoRA serving course.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Measuring forgetting: TOFU, MUSE and the forget-retain tradeoff
md: Unlearning is judged against the retrained model on two axes at once: forget metrics should match it (not undershoot it) and utility should stay near it. Under-unlearning and over-unlearning both leak that the data was there.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: The PE format: headers, sections and what imports reveal
md: Our benign hello.exe imports VirtualProtect and VirtualQuery even though main never calls them: the MinGW-w64 C runtime's startup code uses them. One 'suspicious' import proves nothing. Read imports as a combination, and check what the compiler's runtime adds.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Writing and testing YARA rules
md: A YARA rule is a hypothesis about what makes a family unique. The test set is the evidence. Keep the test files and expected results next to the rule, and rerun them on every change, just like unit tests.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Shortlist then rerank: adaptive retrieval and funnel search
md: The first stage must have high recall (it must not drop the right documents) and the last stage high precision (what it puts on top must be right). Matryoshka prefixes give a cheap high-recall first stage from the same vector the precise stage uses.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: What only RAM knows: Duqu 2.0 and the case for memory
md: Memory-resident code trades persistence for stealth. The defender's answer is to capture memory before anyone reboots, restarts a service or "cleans" the host, and to treat the image as the only copy of that evidence.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Credential artefacts: what memory exposes and how to scope it
md: Scope by exposure, not only by proof of theft. Every account with a session or cached logon on a compromised host goes on the reset list. Memory adds who touched LSASS and how, which tells you whether the attacker could also have reached accounts that were not logged on.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Placement policy: where a block goes decides what survives
md: Separate policy from mechanism. Good policies (address-ordered first fit, best fit, segregated fit approximating best fit) gave near-zero fragmentation on real traces once implementation overheads were removed. The remaining job is to implement such a policy fast, which is what size-classed allocators do.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: From orderings to instructions: x86-64, ARM64, and choosing
md: Start from the happens-before edges your algorithm needs, then pick the weakest ordering that creates each one. Mara Bos suggests treating SeqCst as a warning sign in review: it claims dependence on the order of every SeqCst operation in the program, which is much harder to verify than a single Release/Acquire pair.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: RCU: publish a new version, free the old after a grace period
md: RCU readers pay almost nothing; updaters copy, publish with one pointer store, and defer the free until a grace period has elapsed. A grace period waits only for readers that started before the removal.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Off-by-one: a single byte too far
md: Off-by-one bugs live at the boundary. A test suite that tries length n - 1, n and n + 1 for every buffer finds most of them; AddressSanitizer turns the silent one-byte write into a loud error.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Triplet loss: the margin and easy, semi-hard, hard negatives
md: A triplet only produces gradient when the negative is inside d(a,p) + m. Mining decides which of those active triplets you spend compute on.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Noise, repetitions and when a difference is real
md: Misconception: "overlapping intervals prove the versions are equal". They show you could not detect a difference at this noise level. A smaller real difference may exist; to find it, reduce noise or take more runs.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: MoE routing replay and low-precision RL
md: "BF16 train, FP8 serve" is the lowest-friction mode, but it is not a contract: the docs say there is precision drift between the two paths, and on MoE workloads you should pair it with R3 and optionally TIS.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: LRB: learning to evict like a relaxed Belady
md: The **good decision ratio** (good evictions divided by all evictions) grades each eviction individually. The LRB authors found it correlates strongly with the final byte miss ratio, so they used it to choose features, model, loss and sizes from one simulation pass instead of hours-long full simulations per design.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Dynamic instrumentation with Frida: watch and change a running app
md: On a device its user controls, any value in the app's memory and any boolean the app computes can be read and changed. Design so that changing them gains nothing: keys in secure hardware, decisions on the server.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Why per-head keys and values make the KV cache huge
md: The paper counts cache size in **elements**, regardless of storage precision. Quantizing the cache, storing each element in fewer bits such as FP8 (an 8-bit floating-point format) or lower, is a separate, stackable trick. When comparing headline numbers, check whether both sides use the same precision.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Why MLA can beat GQA at equal cache, and converting models
md: At equal cache, GQA is MLA with selector up-projections, so MLA can only add expressiveness. Converting a trained model to MLA means confining RoPE to a small part, compressing the rest into a latent, and fine-tuning briefly.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: The multi-query pipeline: generate, retrieve in parallel, merge
md: LangChain's synchronous `invoke` searches the generated queries **one after another** in a for loop; only the async `ainvoke` path runs them concurrently with `asyncio.gather`. LlamaIndex runs them concurrently when `use_async=True` (its default). If your multi-query latency grows linearly with N, check which path you are on.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: Latency budgets and phased ranking in real engines
md: Defaults are shallow. Both Elasticsearch's rescore window_size and text_similarity_reranker's rank_window_size default to 10, so an unconfigured reranker can only shuffle the first page. Also keep the window fixed across pages: the docs warn that changing window_size while paginating can make top hits shift.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Why a weight matrix is not a bag of independent numbers
md: Treat a weight matrix as a linear map, not a list of numbers. Its gradient has directions with very different strengths, and these optimizers rebalance those directions instead of rebalancing individual entries.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Scaling Muon to LLMs: weight decay, update RMS and QK-clip
md: Both Moonlight fixes control the *size* of Muon's update, not its direction: decay keeps weights from drifting out of bf16's precise range, and 0.2 sqrt(max(A, B)) gives every matrix the same update RMS as AdamW. QK-clip then caps the one quantity, attention logits, that still grew.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Why 'maximal': kernel, mean-field and feature-learning limits
md: The dichotomy is about the limit as width goes to infinity. A finite SP network does learn features (the paper says so explicitly). The problem is the trend: as you widen an SP model at a stable learning rate, its feature learning fades, and the optimum HPs move. muP keeps feature learning the same at every width, which is why its HPs transfer.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: What muP does not transfer: horizon, weight decay, the SP debate
md: "Per-layer SP beat muP" does not mean muP is wrong. Everett et al. also tune per-layer constants at small scale and transfer them, with per-layer LR exponents; the debate is about which exponents and alignment assumptions hold in practice. Both camps agree that one global LR with SP init is the thing that does not transfer.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: Locks in real systems: kernels, priorities and choices
md: User-space spin locks lack the kernel's guarantee. A user thread cannot disable preemption, so a pure spin lock in an application can always spin against a preempted holder. Prefer the platform mutex, which already spins briefly before sleeping.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Write skew: the bug that snapshot isolation lets through
md: Snapshot isolation prevents conflicts between writes to the same row. Write skew slips through because the conflicting pair is a read and a write to *different* rows.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: Transformer taggers and subword alignment
md:
Two alignment bugs cost real F1 and neither one crashes.

Labelling continuation pieces with `I-X` instead of -100 teaches the model that spans can start and continue inside a word, which leaks into the decoder.

Evaluating on pieces instead of words changes the number of gold entities, so your F1 is not comparable to anyone else's. Map back to words first, then score.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: Why MD5 misses copies, and the average hash that does not
md: A perceptual hash is a summary you **compare**, not an identity you **look up**. Similar images give hashes at a small Hamming distance; the system decides a threshold for what counts as a match.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: Training backends (Automodel, Megatron) and generation backends
md: Training parallelism and generation parallelism are separate settings. For example vLLM's `tensor_parallel_size` is unrelated to Megatron's `tensor_model_parallel_size`. Refit must reshape weights from the trainer's layout into the engine's layout, which is part of why refit transports matter (lesson 4).

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: SYN floods and SYN cookies
md: A SYN flood attacks memory, not bandwidth: a few packets per second can hold a backlog full. SYN cookies move the half-open state into the sequence number the client must echo, so spoofed SYNs cost the server almost nothing.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Wireshark display filters: asking precise questions of packets
md: `ip.addr != X` and `!(ip.addr == X)` both remove every packet to or from X in current Wireshark, but `!==` keeps almost everything. When a filter shows surprisingly many or few packets, check which of the any/all forms you used and whether a hidden existence test removed packets without the field.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: DNS as a control channel: tunnels, generated names and SUNBURST
md: Judge DNS by domain, not by query: unique names per domain, clients per domain, first-seen date, and the answer types (TXT, NXDOMAIN, CNAME chains). Tunnels and DGA-driven channels need a new name for every message; normal software keeps asking for the same few names.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Joining a network: DHCP and ARP
md: "It is on our LAN, so it is trusted" is the assumption ARP and DHCP were built on, and the one attackers exploit. Any device that joins the LAN, including a compromised printer or a guest laptop, can speak these protocols.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Why some memory is farther away than other memory
md: NUMA means the cost of a cache miss depends on which node holds the page. Keep each thread's data on the node where the thread runs.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Keeping threads near their data: pinning, balancing and diagnosis
md: Locality needs both halves: pages on the right node, and threads that stay there. Pin, or let NUMA balancing migrate pages, and verify placement with numa_maps rather than allocation counters.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Scoring a detector: precision, recall, AP and COCO mAP
md: Raising the confidence threshold does not always raise precision. It only helps if the boxes it removes are mostly false positives. A confidently wrong box, like B3 at 0.75, survives every threshold that keeps it.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Committing to object storage: metadata, CAS and fencing
